title: DNS In Depth
description: Learn how the Domain Name System turns human names into machine addresses.

data.text: Every time you type a website name into a browser, the Domain Name System (DNS) quietly translates that human-readable name into an IP address that computers understand. Without DNS, you would have to remember numeric addresses like 142.250.185.14 instead of google.com. DNS is often called the phonebook of the internet, but it is much more than a simple lookup table.

DNS is a distributed, hierarchical database. No single server holds all internet names. Instead, responsibility is split across thousands of servers organized into a tree structure, from root servers down to authoritative name servers for individual domains.

When you request a domain, your device first checks its local cache. If the answer is not there, the query travels through a chain of servers: the recursive resolver, root name servers, top-level domain servers, and finally the authoritative name server that knows the exact IP for the domain.

data.title: DNS Resolution Steps
items: Browser checks its own cache and the operating system cache.
Query is sent to the recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or cloud provider.
Resolver queries a root server to find the .com TLD server.
Resolver queries the .com server to find the domain's authoritative server.
Resolver queries the authoritative server for the exact A or AAAA record.
Answer is cached and returned to your browser.

data.caption: The path of a DNS query from browser to authoritative name server.
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    B[Browser Cache] -->|Miss| R[Recursive Resolver]
    R -->|Query| ROOT[Root Server]
    ROOT -->|Refer| TLD[.com TLD Server]
    TLD -->|Refer| AUTH[Authoritative Server]
    AUTH -->|A/AAAA Record| R
    R -->|Cached Answer| B

data.title: Essential DNS Records
items: A — Maps a domain to an IPv4 address.
AAAA — Maps a domain to an IPv6 address.
CNAME — Aliases one domain to another, like www.example.com to example.com.
MX — Directs email to the correct mail server for a domain.
TXT — Stores arbitrary text, often used for email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).
NS — Lists the name servers responsible for a domain.

data.title: Pro Tip: Flush Local DNS
data.text: When troubleshooting a domain change that does not appear, your local cache may be stale. On Windows, run ipconfig /flushdns. On macOS, run sudo dscacheutil -flushcache. Clearing the cache forces a fresh lookup from authoritative servers.

terms.definition: The DNS server your device contacts first. It does the legwork of querying other servers on your behalf.
The final source of truth for a domain's records. Only it can definitively answer queries for names it controls.
Time To Live — the number of seconds a DNS answer can be cached before it must be rechecked.

data.title: Inspecting DNS Records with dig
data.content: Use the dig command to inspect DNS records for any domain.
data.code:
dig example.com A

; <<>> DiG 9.18.12 <<>> example.com A
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 12345
;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.    3600    IN    A    93.184.216.34

items.question: Why does DNS sometimes take a long time?
items.answer: High latency can come from slow recursive resolvers, misconfigured authoritative servers, or large TTL values keeping stale answers cached.

items.question: What is DNS propagation?
items.answer: When you change a record, every cache in the world must expire before everyone sees the new value. Propagation is the time it takes for all those caches to refresh.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: DNS is a distributed, hierarchical naming system, not a single database.
Resolution involves caches, recursive resolvers, root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative servers.
Different record types serve different purposes, from A records for IPv4 to MX records for email.
TTL controls how long answers are cached and affects propagation speed.
data.takeaway: Understanding DNS is foundational because almost every network failure can be traced back to name resolution.
